pyharp computes radiative fluxes with one of two solvers: the two-stream solver of Toon et al. (`solver: toon`)
and the multi-stream discrete-ordinate solver DISORT (`solver: disort`). This chapter measures how accurate each is
and what it costs. It first fixes a reference: DISORT run with enough streams that adding more no longer changes
the fluxes, validated against published benchmark fluxes and against cases with a closed-form answer. It then
measures Toon against that reference and separates two errors that are easy to confuse: the error of solving the
two-stream equations, which is round-off, and the error of the two-stream approximation itself, which is not. It
ends with the cost per column of each solver. The derivations of the two solvers are not repeated here; they are
the subject of the DISORT and Toon chapters.

### Summary

A two-stream solver can only be judged against something more accurate. In pyharp that is DISORT, which
represents the angular field with $2N$ discrete directions (`nstr` $= 2N$ in the band's YAML) and converges to the
exact plane-parallel solution as $2N$ grows. This section finds the stream count at which DISORT's fluxes stop
changing on the grid of test problems used throughout the chapter, and checks the converged result against the
benchmark fluxes of Garcia and Siewert [@reading25]. That converged run is the reference of
@sec-ch05-toon-accuracy.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** A converged DISORT stream count $2N_{\mathrm{ref}}$; criterion @eq-ch05-reference-change.

**Data.** $F^{+}$ and $F^{-}+F_{\mathrm{dir}}$ at every level, divided by $F_{\mathrm{inc}}$.

**Placement.** A measurement on the solver; nothing in pyharp runs it.

**Activation.** `nstr` in the band YAML, default 4; $2N_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is 64 (beam), 32 (thermal).

**Guarantee / limits.** $d(2N_{\mathrm{ref}}) \le 10^{-5}$; benchmark within $3.8\times10^{-6}$.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $F_{\mathrm{inc}}$ the incident flux that normalises every error [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$];
$d(2N)$ the largest change of the normalised fluxes when the stream count is doubled from $2N$ [-]; $\rho$ the ratio
of two successive changes [-].

The default of 4 streams is not converged: doubling it to 8 moves fluxes on the grid by up to $3\times10^{-2}$ of
the incident flux. A reader who uses DISORT as a reference should set `nstr` to the values found here.

### Derivation

**The quantity that is converged.** For each column of the test grid, DISORT returns at every level $z$ the upward
diffuse flux $F^{+}(z)$ and the total downward flux $F^{-}(z)+F_{\mathrm{dir}}(z)$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$]: pydisort
writes `flup` into channel 0 and `rfldir + rfldn` into channel 1 in `disort_impl`
({{< code src/disort_impl.h disort_impl repo=pydisort >}}). Both are divided by the incident flux

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{\mathrm{inc}} &= \mu_0 F_0 \\
F_{\mathrm{inc}} &= \pi B(T_{\mathrm{s}})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-reference-finc}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-reference-finc check_ch05_convergence.py -->

for a beam and for thermal emission. Here $\mu_0$ [-] is the cosine of the solar zenith angle, $F_0$
[$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$] the beam flux normal to the beam (`fbeam`), $B$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$] the Planck
radiance integrated over the band, and $T_{\mathrm{s}}$ [K] the surface temperature. Write $\hat F_{2N}$ for the
vector of all normalised fluxes of the grid at stream count $2N$: every column, every level, both channels.

**The change on doubling.** The convergence measure is

$$
d(2N) = \max \bigl|\hat F_{2N} - \hat F_{4N}\bigr| ,
$$ {#eq-ch05-reference-change}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-reference-change check_ch05_convergence.py [C6] -->

and $2N_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the smallest stream count with $d(2N_{\mathrm{ref}}) \le 10^{-5}$.

**Why a small change bounds the error.** Let $\hat F_{\infty}$ be the converged answer. Assume that each further
doubling shrinks the change by at least a factor $\rho < 1$, so that for every $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

$$
\max\bigl|\hat F_{2^{k+1}N} - \hat F_{2^{k+2}N}\bigr| \le \rho^{k}\, d(2N) .
$$

Then the error of the run at $2N$ telescopes into a geometric series,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\bigl|\hat F_{2N} - \hat F_{\infty}\bigr|
  &\le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \max\bigl|\hat F_{2^{k+1}N} - \hat F_{2^{k+2}N}\bigr| \\
  &\le d(2N) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \rho^{k} \\
  &= \frac{d(2N)}{1-\rho} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-reference-bound}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-reference-bound check_ch05_convergence.py [C7] -->

The assumption is not proven for DISORT; it is measured. On the grid the last measured ratio is
$\rho = d(64)/d(32) = 0.040$ for the beam and $0.049$ for thermal emission (check lines [C4]-[C5] and
[C11]-[C12]). Taking that ratio for the doublings beyond 128 streams, which were not run for the beam,
@eq-ch05-reference-bound puts the error of the reference within $1.05\,d(2N_{\mathrm{ref}})$.

**The phase function the reference uses.** Every column has a Henyey-Greenstein phase function, whose Legendre
moments are $\chi_l = g^{l}$, with $g$ [-] the asymmetry parameter. `disort_config`
({{< code python/disort.py disort_config repo=pyharp >}}) sets the number of moments equal to `nstr`, and the checks supply
$\chi_1 \ldots \chi_{2N}$. cdisort then applies the $\delta$-M scaling of [@reading05] with truncation fraction
$f = \chi_{2N} = g^{2N}$. It switches the scaling off when $\chi_{2N}$ is zero in every layer (`c_disort`,
{{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}}), so a caller that supplies fewer than `nstr` moments
runs without it.

**The benchmark comparison.** Garcia and Siewert [@reading25, Table 22, p. 480] tabulate the downward flux $q^{+}$,
upward flux $q^{-}$ and net flux $q$ at seven depths for five problems (their Table 21): the Haze L phase function at
$\tau_0 = 1$ and the Cloud C1 phase function at $\tau_0 = 64$, with $\omega = 1$ or $0.9$ and $\mu_0 = 1$ or $0.5$,
beam $\pi F_0 = \pi$, no surface. The measure is the largest relative difference over the non-zero entries,

$$
r_{\mathrm{GS}} = \max \frac{|q_{\mathrm{DISORT}} - q_{\mathrm{GS}}|}{|q_{\mathrm{GS}}|} .
$$ {#eq-ch05-reference-gs}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-reference-gs check_ch05_gs85.py [C7] -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch05-reference-gs benchmark values of Garcia and Siewert 1985, Table 22 -->

The table is printed to six significant figures, so $r_{\mathrm{GS}}$ cannot be shown smaller than about
$5\times10^{-6}$ for an entry near 1.

What is exact and what is truncated: the angular discretisation error of DISORT is truncated at $2N$ streams and is
what @eq-ch05-reference-change measures; the vertical integration of a homogeneous layer is exact in DISORT and in
the test problems, which split each slab into equal homogeneous layers. The checks are
`check_ch05_convergence.py` and `check_ch05_gs85.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

The test grid is a set of homogeneous slabs. For the beam: total optical depth
$\tau_0 \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10\}$, single-scattering albedo $\omega \in \{0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, 1\}$,
$g \in \{0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.85\}$, $\mu_0 \in \{0.2, 0.5, 1\}$ and Lambertian surface albedo $A_s \in \{0, 0.4\}$:
864 columns of two equal layers, with fluxes at the top, the middle and the surface. For thermal emission: the same
$\tau_0$ and $g$, $\omega \in \{0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 0.99\}$, $A_s \in \{0, 0.4\}$, the band 500 to
1000 $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, temperature linear in optical depth from 200 K at the top to 300 K at the bottom, a surface
of emissivity $1 - A_s$ at 300 K, and no radiation entering at the top: 240 columns of eight layers. All columns of
one stream count run in one batched call.

@fig-ch05-reference-convergence shows both measurements. The steps of one evaluation:

1. Build the property tensor of each column, bottom layer first, with optical depth, $\omega$ and the moments
   $\chi_1 \ldots \chi_{2N}$; pyharp's arrays run from the surface up, unlike cdisort's, and `disort_impl` reverses
   them ({{< code src/disort_impl.h disort_impl repo=pydisort >}}).
2. Configure DISORT through `disort_config` ({{< code python/disort.py disort_config repo=pyharp >}}) with flags
   `lamber,quiet,onlyfl` (and `planck` for thermal emission) and `upward(True)`.
3. Solve. cdisort replaces $\omega = 1$ by $1 - 100\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$, with $\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ the
   double-precision machine epsilon, to avoid the degenerate eigenproblem (`c_disort`,
   {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}}).
4. Repeat for $2N = 4, 8, \ldots, 128$ and evaluate @eq-ch05-reference-change between neighbours.

There is no iteration and no stopping criterion: each run is a direct solve.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **The default `nstr` of 4 is not a reference.** It changes by up to $3\times10^{-2}$ of the incident flux on
  doubling; tests that compare against it inherit that error (@sec-ch05-toon-accuracy, Tests).
- **More streams is not always better.** At 256 streams the benchmark difference rises again, to
  $3.90\times10^{-3}$ for problem 2, with the same moment table.[^ch05-ref-gs] The cause is not measured here;
  128 streams is the largest count this section relies on.
- **Layers below absorption depth 10 are cut.** For a beam with more than one layer, cdisort stops the solution
  where the absorption optical depth reaches 10 (`c_disort_set`,
  {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort_set repo=pydisort >}}) and sets the fluxes below to zero. The loss is at
  most $e^{-10} = 4.54\times10^{-5}$ of the incident flux (@sec-ch05-analytic).
- **Untested combinations.** Only Henyey-Greenstein moments, one band, homogeneous slabs, Lambertian surfaces and
  azimuth-integrated fluxes are covered; intensities and the intensity corrections that `create_disort_config_sw`
  ({{< code src/radiation/disort_config.cpp create_disort_config_sw repo=pyharp >}}) switches on are not.
:::

### Summary

A few radiative-transfer problems have an exact answer that needs no solver: a beam crossing an absorbing slab, a
slab that only emits, and the bookkeeping of energy between the top, the column and the surface. This section runs
both solvers (`solver: toon` and `solver: disort`) on those problems. They check the parts of each solver that do
not depend on the scattering approximation, and they confirm that the DISORT reference of @sec-ch05-reference is
right where an exact answer exists.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Closed forms @eq-ch05-analytic-beam, @eq-ch05-analytic-e3; closure @eq-ch05-analytic-closure.

**Data.** Fluxes at every level of single- and multi-layer slabs, normalised by $F_{\mathrm{inc}}$.

**Placement.** A measurement on the solvers; nothing in pyharp runs it.

**Activation.** `solver` in the band YAML (`toon` or `disort`); required, no default.

**Guarantee / limits.** Beam to $2\times10^{-16}$; Toon emission to $3.2\times10^{-4}$.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $A_{\mathrm{col}}$ the flux absorbed in the column [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$]; $I_s$ the radiance
leaving a Lambertian surface [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$]; $E_3$ the third
exponential integral, $E_3(x) = \int_0^1 \mu\, e^{-x/\mu}\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ [-]; $F_{\mathrm{net}}$, $J$, $A_s$ as
in the ch2 notation; $F_{\mathrm{inc}}$ as in @eq-ch05-reference-finc.

### Derivation

**A beam in an absorbing slab.** With no scattering ($\omega = 0$) the beam loses energy along its path only. A
beam of flux $F_0$ normal to its direction, entering at $\tau = 0$ with cosine $\mu_0$, keeps the fraction
$e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ after the slant path $\tau/\mu_0$, so the downward flux on a horizontal surface is

$$
F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau) = \mu_0 F_0\, e^{-\tau/\mu_0} ,
$$ {#eq-ch05-analytic-beam}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-analytic-beam check_ch05_analytic.py [C1] -->

with $\tau$ [-] the optical depth measured down from the top, and no diffuse flux arises. Toon's shortwave kernel
computes @eq-ch05-analytic-beam directly when every layer has $\omega \le 10^{-12}$ and the surface is black (the
branch on `all_zero_w` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave`,
{{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).

**The beam reflected by a Lambertian surface.** A surface of albedo $A_s$ [-] at $\tau_0$ reflects the flux
$A_s F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_0)$ isotropically, with radiance $I_s = A_s F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_0)/\pi$. Through an
absorbing path of vertical optical depth $\tau_0 - \tau$ the radiance in direction $\mu$ keeps
$e^{-(\tau_0-\tau)/\mu}$, so the
upward flux at $\tau$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{+}(\tau) &= 2\pi \int_0^1 I_s\, e^{-(\tau_0-\tau)/\mu}\, \mu\,\mathrm{d}\mu \\
            &= 2\pi I_s\, E_3(\tau_0 - \tau) \\
            &= 2 A_s F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_0)\, E_3(\tau_0 - \tau) .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-analytic-reflect}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-analytic-reflect check_ch05_analytic.py [C14] -->

**A slab that only emits.** An isothermal slab of optical depth $\tau_0$, Planck radiance $B$ and no scattering,
with no radiation entering at the top, sends down along $\mu$ the radiance
$I^{-}(\tau_0,\mu) = B\,(1 - e^{-\tau_0/\mu})$. The downward flux at its bottom is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{-}(\tau_0) &= 2\pi \int_0^1 B\,(1 - e^{-\tau_0/\mu})\, \mu\,\mathrm{d}\mu \\
              &= \pi B - 2\pi B\, E_3(\tau_0) \\
              &= \pi B\,\bigl(1 - 2E_3(\tau_0)\bigr) .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-analytic-e3}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-analytic-e3 check_ch05_analytic.py [C21] -->

Over a black surface at the same temperature the column is in equilibrium and the upward flux is $\pi B$ at every
level. Toon's thermal kernel integrates over $\mu$ with five Gauss points (`uarr`, `wuarr` in
`toon_mckay89_longwave`, {{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}}), so
@eq-ch05-analytic-e3 measures that quadrature.

**Energy closure.** Write the net flux upward-positive, $F_{\mathrm{net}} = F^{+} - F^{-} - F_{\mathrm{dir}}$
[$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$], and $J$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$] for the mean radiance including the beam. Integrating
the radiative-transfer equation over all directions gives the divergence of the net flux, and integrating that over
the column gives the absorbed flux:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{net}}}{\mathrm{d}\tau} &= (1-\omega)\, 4\pi J \\
A_{\mathrm{col}} &= F_{\mathrm{net}}(\tau_0) - F_{\mathrm{net}}(0) = \int_0^{\tau_0} (1-\omega)\, 4\pi J\,\mathrm{d}\tau .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-analytic-closure}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-analytic-closure check_ch05_analytic.py [C25] -->

Two consequences are checked. With $\omega = 1$ the right side vanishes, so $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the same at every
level. With $\omega < 1$, the flux drop $F_{\mathrm{net}}(\tau_0) - F_{\mathrm{net}}(0)$ and the integral of the
mean radiance are two independent routes to $A_{\mathrm{col}}$. A third line, reflected plus column-absorbed plus
surface-absorbed equal to incident, is an identity of these definitions once the top boundary has
$F^{-}(0) = 0$ and $F_{\mathrm{dir}}(0) = \mu_0 F_0$; it therefore checks that boundary condition. The surface itself
must satisfy $F^{+}(\tau_0) = A_s\,\bigl(F^{-}(\tau_0) + F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_0)\bigr)$.

Every expression above is exact; nothing in this section is truncated except the solvers' own discretisations,
which are what the comparison measures. The check is `check_ch05_analytic.py` (Tests layer).

### Summary

Toon's solver replaces the angular field by two hemispheric fluxes and solves the resulting pair of linear
differential equations exactly in every homogeneous layer. Its fluxes therefore differ from the true ones for two
separate reasons: the round-off of solving those equations, and the approximation of replacing many directions by
two. This section measures both on the chapter's grid. The first is at round-off; the second is up to
$8.7\times10^{-2}$ of the incident flux, with a median of $1.1\times10^{-3}$. The section closes with tolerances for
pyharp's tests that follow from these numbers, and with one input on which the solver fails: a single-scattering
albedo of exactly one.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Split Toon's flux error into numerical and approximation parts, @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-split.

**Data.** Toon and DISORT fluxes on the grid of @sec-ch05-reference.

**Placement.** A measurement on the solver; nothing in pyharp runs it.

**Activation.** `solver: toon` in the band YAML; `flags` for thermal options.

**Guarantee / limits.** Round-off for $\omega < 1$; wrong at $\omega = 1$ exactly.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $e^{\mathrm{num}}$, $e^{\mathrm{app}}$, $e^{\mathrm{tot}}$ the numerical, approximation and total
flux errors [-]; $r$ the fractional error [-]; $\mathsf M$ the $3\times3$ matrix of the shortwave system [-];
$\mathbf v$ its state vector; $x$ the unknown upward flux at the top. The two-stream symbols $\gamma_1$ to
$\gamma_4$, $\lambda$ and $\Gamma$, the scaled variables $\omega'$, $\tau'$, $g'$, and the margin $\delta\omega$ are
those of the ch2 notation.

These tolerances are proposed for `tests/test_toon.py` in place of the 20 % gate against 4-stream DISORT: 10 % on
shortwave fluxes against DISORT at 64 streams, $10^{-5}$ on non-scattering thermal fluxes, 5 % on scattering thermal
fluxes, and a new numerical gate of $10^{-12}$ against the exact two-stream solution. The Tests layer gives the
measurement behind each.

### Derivation

**The equations Toon solves.** In each layer pyharp first applies the $\delta$-Eddington scaling, which moves the
forward peak of the phase function into the direct beam [@reading06]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\omega' &= \frac{(1-g^2)\,\omega}{1-\omega g^2} \\
\Delta\tau' &= (1-\omega g^2)\,\Delta\tau \\
g' &= \frac{g}{1+g} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-scaling}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-scaling check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C1] -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-scaling delta-Eddington scaling of Joseph et al. 1976 -->

with $\Delta\tau$ [-] the layer optical thickness. It then uses the quadrature closure of Toon et al.
[@reading02, Table 1, p. 16,289], with $\mu_0$ the cosine of the solar zenith angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1 &= \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\bigl(2 - \omega'(1+g')\bigr) \\
\gamma_2 &= \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\omega'(1-g') \\
\gamma_3 &= \tfrac12\,\bigl(1 - \sqrt3\, g'\mu_0\bigr) \\
\gamma_4 &= 1 - \gamma_3 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-gamma}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-gamma check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C1] -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-gamma Toon et al. 1989, Table 1 -->

@eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-scaling and @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-gamma are computed in `toon_mckay89_shortwave`
({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}). With $\tau'$ the scaled optical
depth from the top, the diffuse fluxes then obey [@reading02, eqs. 11-14, p. 16,289]

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}F^{+}}{\mathrm{d}\tau'} &= \gamma_1 F^{+} - \gamma_2 F^{-} - \gamma_3\,\omega' F_0\, e^{-\tau'/\mu_0} \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}F^{-}}{\mathrm{d}\tau'} &= \gamma_2 F^{+} - \gamma_1 F^{-} + \gamma_4\,\omega' F_0\, e^{-\tau'/\mu_0} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C1] -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode Toon et al. 1989, eqs. 11-14 -->

with no diffuse radiation entering at the top, $F^{-}(0) = 0$, and a Lambertian surface at $\tau_0'$,
$F^{+}(\tau_0') = A_s\bigl(F^{-}(\tau_0') + \mu_0 F_0\, e^{-\tau_0'/\mu_0}\bigr)$. pyharp solves
@eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode layer by layer with exponentials $e^{\pm\lambda\tau'}$, $\lambda^2 = \gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2$,
joined by a tridiagonal system (`toon_mckay89_shortwave`,
{{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}); the solution method itself is the
subject of the Toon chapter.

**An independent exact solution.** For a homogeneous slab, collect $\mathbf v = (F^{+}, F^{-}, e^{-\tau'/\mu_0})$
with $F_0 = 1$. @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode becomes the linear system $\mathrm{d}\mathbf v/\mathrm{d}\tau' =
\mathsf M\,\mathbf v$, with

$$
\mathsf M = \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1 & -\gamma_2 & -\gamma_3\,\omega' \\ \gamma_2 & -\gamma_1 & \gamma_4\,\omega' \\ 0 & 0 & -1/\mu_0 \end{pmatrix} .
$$

Its solution from the top is $\mathbf v(\tau') = \exp(\mathsf M\tau')\,\mathbf v(0)$ with $\mathbf v(0) = (x, 0, 1)$,
where $x$ is the unknown upward flux at the top. Write $\mathsf P = \exp(\mathsf M\tau_0')$. The surface condition
is linear in $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{11}x + P_{13} &= A_s\,\bigl(P_{21}x + P_{23} + \mu_0 P_{33}\bigr) \\
x &= -\frac{P_{13} - A_s P_{23} - A_s \mu_0 P_{33}}{P_{11} - A_s P_{21}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-shoot}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-shoot check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C1] -->

Shooting from the top amplifies round-off by $e^{\lambda\tau_0'}$, which reaches $e^{35}$ on the grid, so the check
evaluates @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-shoot in 50-digit arithmetic (`exact_sw` in
`derivation-checks/check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py`); the result is exact to double precision.

**The error split.** With $\hat F$ fluxes normalised by $F_{\mathrm{inc}}$ (@eq-ch05-reference-finc),

$$
\begin{aligned}
e^{\mathrm{tot}} &= \hat F_{\mathrm{Toon}} - \hat F_{\mathrm{DISORT}} \\
                 &= \bigl(\hat F_{\mathrm{Toon}} - \hat F_{\mathrm{exact}}\bigr) + \bigl(\hat F_{\mathrm{exact}} - \hat F_{\mathrm{DISORT}}\bigr) \\
                 &= e^{\mathrm{num}} + e^{\mathrm{app}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-split}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-split check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C3] -->

where $\hat F_{\mathrm{exact}}$ solves @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode exactly and $\hat F_{\mathrm{DISORT}}$ is the
reference of @sec-ch05-reference. The reference's own error, below $1.05\times10^{-5}$ by @eq-ch05-reference-bound,
is part of $e^{\mathrm{app}}$. Toon et al. judge accuracy by the fractional error relative to the exact value
[@reading02, p. 16,294]; on fluxes of at least 1 % of the incident flux it is

$$
r = \frac{|e^{\mathrm{tot}}|}{|\hat F_{\mathrm{DISORT}}|} .
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-frac}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-frac check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C35] -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-frac fractional error of Toon et al. 1989, p. 16,294 -->

**Why $\omega = 1$ breaks the kernel.** At $\omega = 1$, @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-scaling gives $\omega' = 1$ for any
$g$, and @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-gamma gives $\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}(1-g') \equiv \gamma$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda^2 &= \gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2 = 0 \\
\Gamma &= \frac{\gamma_1 - \lambda}{\gamma_2} = 1 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-degenerate}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-degenerate check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py [C2] -->

The homogeneous part of @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode becomes $\mathrm{d}F^{\pm}/\mathrm{d}\tau' = \gamma\,(F^{+} -
F^{-})$. Subtracting the two lines gives $\mathrm{d}(F^{+} - F^{-})/\mathrm{d}\tau' = 0$, so its general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{+} - F^{-} &= c \\
F^{-} &= b + \gamma c\,\tau' ,
\end{aligned}
$$

with two constants $b$ and $c$. The kernel's basis is $F^{+} = k_1 e^{\lambda\tau'} + \Gamma k_2 e^{-\lambda\tau'}$,
$F^{-} = \Gamma k_1 e^{\lambda\tau'} + k_2 e^{-\lambda\tau'}$ [@reading02, eqs. 19-20, p. 16,290]. At
$\lambda = 0$ and $\Gamma = 1$ both terms are the constant $k_1 + k_2$, so the basis spans only $c = 0$: it has lost
the mode that carries a net diffuse flux. The two boundary conditions can then not both be met. Toon et al. avoid
the limit by taking $1 - \omega_0$ equal to ten times the machine precision [@reading02, p. 16,291];
`RadiationBandImpl::forward` clamps $\omega \le 1 - \delta\omega$ with $\delta\omega = 10^{-12}$ in double and
$10^{-6}$ in single precision ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}), but the
kernel itself applies no margin. That the lost mode is the cause is read from the code; the measured symptom in the
Tests layer, equal upward and downward fluxes at every level, is what it predicts.

What is exact and what is truncated: @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-shoot is exact; Toon's kernel is exact for
@eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode up to round-off for $\omega < 1$; the truncation is the two-stream closure, which
$e^{\mathrm{app}}$ measures. The check is `check_ch05_toon_vs_disort.py` (Tests layer).

**Thermal emission.** Toon's thermal kernel does not solve a two-stream equation for the fluxes it returns: it
uses the hemispheric-mean two-stream solution only for the scattering source and integrates the emergent radiance
over five Gauss directions [@reading02, eqs. 52-56, p. 16,293]. Its numerical part is therefore bounded in two
ways that need no exact solution: a homogeneous isothermal slab gives the same fluxes as one layer or as sixteen,
and its band Planck integral agrees with DISORT's on an opaque slab. Everything else in its error is approximation.

: Tests of Toon's accuracy. {#tbl-ch05-toon-accuracy-tests}

**Numerical part.** Over the 720 shortwave columns with $\omega < 1$, $\max|e^{\mathrm{num}}| = 2.7\times10^{-15}$
of the incident flux, and the largest fractional numerical error is $1.0\times10^{-13}$. Toon's kernel solves
@eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-ode to round-off, so $e^{\mathrm{tot}} = e^{\mathrm{app}}$ to every digit shown below. The
thermal kernel's multi-layer invariance holds to $2.9\times10^{-13}$ of $\pi B$, and its Planck integrals agree with
DISORT's to $4.8\times10^{-7}$ (300 K) and $4.2\times10^{-8}$ (200 K).[^ch05-toon-run]

**Approximation part, shortwave.** Over all fluxes with $\omega < 1$ the largest error is $8.65\times10^{-2}$ of
the incident flux and the median $1.06\times10^{-3}$; the fractional error of @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-frac has median
$6.6\times10^{-3}$ and maximum 0.49. By regime the errors are those of @tbl-ch05-toon-accuracy-regimes.

At $\mu_0 = 0.2$ the median is $2.9\times10^{-3}$, at
$\mu_0 \ge 0.5$ it is $6.8\times10^{-4}$. For the boundary quantities the largest errors are $8.6\times10^{-2}$ in
reflectance, $8.7\times10^{-2}$ in transmitted flux and $5.5\times10^{-2}$ in column absorption. Of the 3569 fluxes
of at least 1 % of the incident flux, 461 have $r > 10\,\%$: 344 of them are upward fluxes and 243 are at
$\mu_0 = 0.2$. The largest, $r = 0.49$, is the mid-level upward flux of $0.018$ of the incident flux at
$\tau_0 = 10$, $\omega = 0.9$, $g = 0.85$, $\mu_0 = 0.2$.[^ch05-toon-run]

**Approximation part, thermal.** With `hard_surface`, the largest error is $4.8\times10^{-2}$ of $\pi B(300\,K)$ and
the median $6.5\times10^{-4}$; adding `delta_eddington_lw` lowers them to $3.5\times10^{-2}$ and $5.6\times10^{-4}$.
Without scattering the error is below $2\times10^{-4}$ for all optical depths. The largest error is in thick slabs
with $\omega = 0.9$ to $0.99$, where the fractional error reaches 0.12 (0.10 with `delta_eddington_lw`).[^ch05-toon-run]

**Against Toon et al.** On the five Garcia-Siewert problems, with the asymmetry parameters Toon et al. used (0.794
and 0.848) and $\omega = 1$ run at $1 - 10^{-12}$, pyharp reproduces the approximate reflected and diffusely
transmitted fluxes of their Table 4 [@reading02, p. 16,295] to every printed digit: the largest difference is
$3.5\times10^{-4}$. With $g = \chi_1$ of the benchmark moment table, Toon's errors against the exact Table 22 values
are 0.1 % to 8.6 %, except the diffuse transmission of the thick absorbing cloud (problem 5, $4.7\times10^{-7}$ of
the incident flux), which is off by 78 %.[^ch05-toon-gs] Toon et al. state that the errors "are typically less than
10 % unless the flux or heating rate is 1 % or less" of the incident flux [@reading02, p. 16,296]. On this grid
that holds for the median, not for every flux: 13 % of the fluxes above 1 % of the incident flux have errors above
10 %, almost all small upward fluxes at low sun and strong forward scattering.

**Tolerances for `tests/test_toon.py`.** Measured on the cases those tests run:[^ch05-toon-run]

- `test_toon_sw_vs_disort`: measured 9.2 % against 4 streams and 8.4 % against the reference; proposed 10 %,
  against DISORT at 64 streams, which covers 8.4 % while 4 streams is not converged.
- `test_toon_lw_isothermal`: measured $4.8\times10^{-7}$ against both; proposed $10^{-5}$, since only the Planck
  integrals differ.
- `test_toon_lw_isothermal_scattering`: measured 3.4 % against 4 streams and 3.5 % against the reference; proposed
  5 %.
- New, a numerical gate: measured $2.7\times10^{-15}$; proposed $10^{-12}$, 100 times round-off.

The thermal tolerance of 20 % hides any regression five orders of
magnitude below it. Only the numerical gate can see an implementation error smaller than the two-stream error.

All Toon measurements run on the CPU in double precision; CUDA is the subject of the GPU chapter.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **Candidate defect: $\omega = 1$ exactly in a direct call.** `ToonMcKay89` called directly with $\omega = 1$
  returns equal upward and downward fluxes at every level. On the grid the error reaches 1.37 of the incident
  flux, and on the thick conservative cloud (problem 4) the diffuse transmission is 100 % off. A band run through
  `RadiationBandImpl::forward` is not affected, because it clamps $\omega$ first
  ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}). The cause, the lost mode of
  @eq-ch05-toon-accuracy-degenerate, is read from the code. This is one run; it stays a candidate until a second, independent run agrees.[^ch05-toon-run]
- **Small upward fluxes at low sun.** Fractional errors reach 49 % on upward fluxes of 1 % to 5 % of the incident
  flux at $\mu_0 = 0.2$ and $g = 0.85$; tolerances on such fluxes must be absolute, not relative.
- **Reflecting surfaces.** Over a Lambertian surface Toon carries the reflected field with two streams and misses
  the exact upward flux by $6.2\times10^{-3}$ of the incident flux even without scattering (@sec-ch05-analytic), as
  Toon et al. note [@reading02, p. 16,291].
- **Not measured.** Inhomogeneous columns, the `zenith_correction` flag, `top_emission_flag` other than 0, thermal
  runs without `hard_surface` against DISORT, and single precision.
:::

### Summary

The accuracy of @sec-ch05-toon-accuracy has a price, and this section measures it: the CPU time to compute the
fluxes of one atmospheric column with Toon and with DISORT at several stream counts. Toon solves one tridiagonal
system per column; DISORT solves an eigenproblem in every layer and a banded linear system whose size grows with
the stream count. On one host and one thread, DISORT at the 64 streams of the reference costs about 3700 times Toon.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** CPU time per column of Toon and of DISORT against the stream count $2N$; scaling @eq-ch05-cost-scaling.

**Data.** 256 columns of 50 layers per call, random optical properties; time per column [$\mu$s].

**Placement.** A measurement; nothing in pyharp runs it.

**Activation.** `solver` and `nstr` in the band YAML; thread count from torch.

**Guarantee / limits.** One host; times include building the inputs and the solver object of each call.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $c$ the wall-clock cost per column [s]; $L$ the number of layers (count); $p$ the fitted exponent of $c$
against the stream count [-].

### Derivation

**Toon.** For $L$ layers Toon's shortwave kernel evaluates closed-form coefficients in every layer and solves one
tridiagonal system of order $2L$ by elimination (`toon_mckay89_shortwave`,
{{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}). Each step is a fixed number of
operations per layer, so the cost is proportional to $L$ and independent of any stream count.

**DISORT.** With $2N$ streams cdisort solves, in every layer, an eigenproblem of order $N$ for the homogeneous
solution (`c_solve_eigen`, {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve_eigen repo=pydisort >}}), and then one banded
system for the constants of integration of all layers (`c_solve0`,
{{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve0 repo=pydisort >}}). The eigenproblem costs of order $N^3$ per layer. The
banded system has order $2NL$ and a bandwidth of order $2N$; elimination costs the order times the square of the
bandwidth. Together,

$$
c_{\mathrm{DISORT}} \propto L\,N^{3} ,
$$ {#eq-ch05-cost-scaling}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch05-cost-scaling check_ch05_cost.py [C11] -->

for large $N$; for small $N$ the operations that grow as $N$ and $N^2$ (setting up the source terms and the
quadrature) still weigh, so the measured exponent $p$ approaches 3 from below.

**Batching.** Both solvers run all columns and wavelengths of one call through one tensor iterator; on the CPU the
columns are distributed over torch's threads (`call_toon89_sw_cpu`,
{{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}). The time per column is the call time divided by
the number of columns.

What is exact and what is approximate: @eq-ch05-cost-scaling is an operation count, not a measured law; the
exponent is fitted below from at least three stream counts. The check is `check_ch05_cost.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

Each measurement runs 256 columns of 50 layers with optical depths log-uniform between $10^{-3}$ and 1 per layer,
$\omega$ between 0 and 0.99, $g$ between 0 and 0.85, $\mu_0$ between 0.1 and 1 and $A_s$ between 0 and 0.5 (seed 0),
and takes the best of three calls. It is repeated with one thread and with torch's default thread count. Every
call builds its input tensors and a new solver object, as a caller with a new set of columns would.

With one thread, Toon takes $4.0\,\mu$s per column for the shortwave and $21\,\mu$s for thermal emission. DISORT
takes $43\,\mu$s at 4 streams, $144\,\mu$s at 8, $525\,\mu$s at 16, $2.50$ ms at 32 and $14.8$ ms at 64, that is 11,
36, 130, 620 and 3684 times Toon's shortwave time. The fitted exponent $p$ of @eq-ch05-cost-scaling is 1.81 over 4,
8 and 16 streams and 2.41 over 16, 32 and 64. With the default 16 threads Toon takes $1.2\,\mu$s and DISORT $5.2\,\mu$s
at 4 streams and $1.47$ ms at 64.[^ch05-cost-run] The thermal DISORT times are within 10 % of the shortwave ones at
every stream count.

The times are of one host and one run; a different processor, thread count or column size changes them. What they
show that does not depend on the host is the ratio: a converged DISORT reference is three to four orders of
magnitude more expensive than Toon.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **One host, CPU only.** Times on CUDA, and the CUDA support of each solver, are the subject of the GPU chapter.
- **Included overheads.** Each timing includes building the solver object and the input tensors; a caller that
  reuses one solver object for many calls pays less per call. That split is not measured.
- **Not measured.** Column counts other than 256, layer counts other than 50, and repeated timings with their
  spread.
:::
